sketch.title: Funnel into case synthesis
sketch.caption: A funnel-into-chain: historical puzzle and method narrow into a large case collection (scientists, then other trained observers), which is distilled into a statistical synopsis and tested against six landmark cases, ending in a call for coordinated research.

scenes.title: Overview

items.text: Ball lightning: a century of unexplained sightings
Method: compile trained-observer reports since cameras rarely catch it
Synopsis: consistent thunderstorm timing, wide variation in size and behavior

scenes.caption: The piece narrows from background and method into a large body of eyewitness cases, then widens back out into synthesis, notable benchmarks, and a forward-looking conclusion.

scenes.title: Scientists' own sightings

items.text: Durward: cockpit fireball and Scotland gatepost strike
Jennison's glowing sphere on a night flight
Dmitriev measures elevated ozone after a ball's passage
Wittmann, age 9: ball fragments into smaller melting spheres

scenes.caption: A spine of firsthand accounts by physicists, engineers, and physicians spans 1868 to 2002, each adding detail on speed, damage, or chemical traces.

scenes.title: Six landmark cases

items.text: Richmann's 1753 death: myth, not ball lightning
Charcot's patient D-cy: paralysis and trauma
Dorstone tub: boiling water, an energy-density puzzle
Poughquag glass door fluoresces under the ball's light
Cen's spectroscopy and Nikitin's video triangulation

scenes.caption: Across two and a half centuries, these benchmark cases move from a mythic misattribution to cases with physical traces and, finally, instrumented data.

plates.title: The Chain of Witnesses
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page on aged vellum, ink-and-wash in sepia with faded indigo and ochre, eleven round medallions strung top to bottom by a thin hand-drawn chain-line, each medallion in its own thin ink ring, a gothic blackletter caption lettered beneath each one in capitals and nothing else written anywhere on the page. At the top: a rain-soaked Milan street, figures pointing up at a reddish-yellow ball of fire drifting past a window toward a church tower, captioned BALL OF FIRE OVER MILAN. Below it, a wall of tiny identical sky-photographs with a magnifying glass over two marked frames among thousands, captioned 12 000 PHOTOGRAPHS SEARCHED. The chain then passes into a loosely drawn enclosure labelled by composition alone (no lettering) holding three medallions in sequence: a scholar at a Vienna window watching a ball hover beyond the glass (HAIDINGER AT THE WINDOW); a physicist at an institute window with chalk trajectory lines tracking a streak of light toward a barn (GERLACH TIMES THE FIREBALL); and a boy in the street watching a falling sphere shatter into smaller glowing spheres (SPHERE SPLITS OVER THE STREET). The chain exits this enclosure into a second enclosure of two medallions: a mountain station shed with a ball of fire passing through the woodshed past a startled worker (FIREBALL IN THE WOODSHED), and a man sitting up in bed watching a small orange sphere hover near the foot of the bed (SPHERE BY THE BEDSIDE). Next, a single medallion shows a measuring rule spanning a dot to a house-sized sphere (SIZES FROM 1.5 CM TO 15 M). The chain then enters a third enclosure of two medallions: a framed engraving of a scientist struck down beneath an imagined fireball (THE ENGRAVING OF RICHMANN'S DEATH), and a steel test-plate under triggered lightning forming a small glowing ball while researchers photograph it (33 CM BALL FROM TRIGGERED LIGHTNING). The chain ends at the bottom in a single medallion of researchers fitting drawings and photographs into a growing bound ledger (BUILDING THE CASE DATABASE). Aged parchment background with soft foxing at the edges, no colour beyond muted earth tones, generous space between medallions, no decorative border beasts or filler scrollwork beyond a plain ruled frame.

plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page on aged vellum, ink-and-wash in sepia with faded indigo and ochre, six round medallions strung top to bottom by a thin hand-drawn chain-line, each in its own ink ring with a gothic blackletter caption beneath in capitals, nothing else lettered anywhere. The chain descends to a man on a rural road during a storm, recoiling from a whirling fireball shaped like a small barrel hovering just ahead of him (THE WHIRLING BEER-BARREL FIREBALL). Next, a cottage with a scorched window frame and severed wires, a red-hot ball plunging into a wash tub of water beneath the sill, steam rising (THE BALL IN THE WATER TUB). Below that, a woman seated in a parked car at night, watching a glowing yellow ball glowing within the glass of her front porch door (FIERY BALL IN THE GLASS DOOR). Then a wide test field at dusk, a rocket trailing a wire toward storm clouds, triggered lightning striking a row of different ground materials while researchers crouch nearby with cameras (LIGHTNING TRIGGERED ONTO 100 SUBSTANCES). The chain ends with two cameras fitted with diffraction gratings aimed at a distant hillside crossed by a power line, recording a glowing ball beside a lightning channel with a faint rainbow-streaked spectrum trailing beside it (SPECTRUM OF THE QINGHAI FIREBALL). Aged parchment background, soft foxing at the corners, muted earth-tone washes only, medallions large enough to read clearly, generous spacing down the page, no decorative beasts or filler scrollwork beyond a plain ruled border.

questions.question: In Arago's original sense, what kind of phenomenon does the term 'ball lightning' refer to?
questions.referenceAnswer: A still-unexplained group of short-lived, metastable glowing phenomena in atmospheric electricity, which appear seemingly at random, last only a few seconds, and disappear with or without leaving traces.

evidence.quote: stands for a still unexplained group of metastable luminous phenomena in atmospheric electricity. Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without.

questions.question: What did lightning researchers Rakov and Uman say was still missing despite thousands of eyewitness reports of ball lightning?
questions.premise: Ball lightning appears seemingly random and lasts only seconds, usually leaving little trace.
questions.referenceAnswer: They said there was little, if any, real scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other recordings, even though almost 5000 witness reports existed.

evidence.quote: a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.

questions.question: Given this lack of hard evidence, why did the author focus his review specifically on reports from scientists and other trained professionals?
questions.premise: Despite thousands of eyewitness reports, there is little real scientific documentation of ball lightning.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because directly monitoring the phenomenon is almost impossible, and earlier large eyewitness databases, like Rayle's and McNally's, never even recorded the observers' professions or training, so he sought reports from people whose expertise might make their testimony more reliable.

evidence.quote: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal

questions.question: Besides scientists, what other category of trained observer does the article highlight as valuable for documenting ball lightning, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Weather observers at meteorological stations, because they are trained and well positioned to notice and record transient weather phenomena as part of their regular duties.

evidence.quote: Weather observers of meteorological stations are trained and predestined to see and report transient weather phenomena.

questions.question: What concern does the article raise about the future availability of such weather-observer sightings?
questions.premise: Weather observers are trained and well positioned to notice transient weather phenomena like ball lightning.
questions.referenceAnswer: Weather services are increasingly automating stations and removing on-site observers for economic reasons, which eliminates the chance of high-quality human observations of rare events like ball lightning.

evidence.quote: The tendency of weather services to do without observers and automate synoptic stations (including German mountaintop observatories) may be justified from an economic standpoint, but it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning.

questions.question: In the author's correlation study of 34 central European ball lightning events with lightning-detection data, what was surprising about the share of positive lightning strokes?
questions.referenceAnswer: Nineteen of the correlated strokes were positive versus 15 negative, an unexpectedly high proportion of positive strokes, since standard detection records normally show positive lightning as much rarer, around 17% of events.

evidence.quote: in a 10-year interval, ALDIS recorded 17 % positive lightning events at Austria

questions.question: Across the 41 scientist and professional case reports, what range of object sizes and durations was recorded?
questions.referenceAnswer: Reported sizes ranged from 1.5 cm to 15 m, mostly under 20 cm but with several cases over 1 m, while durations ranged from 1.5 to 180 seconds, mostly under 3 seconds but with a mean of 19.5 seconds.

evidence.quote: Reported object sizes (28 cases) range from 1.5 cm to 15 m, with the maximum below 20 cm and several cases over 1 m.

questions.question: What proportion of the 41 cases were linked to a thunderstorm?
questions.referenceAnswer: About 73% occurred during a thunderstorm, 10% just before or after one, and 17% had no thunderstorm connection at all.

evidence.quote: 73 % occurred within thunderstorms, 10 % before or after, and 17 % without a connection.

questions.question: What conclusion have some researchers, such as Rakov and Uman, drawn from this wide variation in case details?
questions.premise: About 73% of the 41 cases occurred during a thunderstorm, but 17% had no thunderstorm connection, and sizes and durations varied enormously from case to case.
questions.referenceAnswer: They have concluded that there may be more than one type of ball lightning, produced by more than one underlying mechanism.

evidence.quote: There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated
some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model. This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.

questions.question: In Martin Uman's 2008 field experiments at Camp Blanding, what did triggering lightning strikes into various ground materials produce, and how did the researchers characterize these results?
questions.referenceAnswer: The strikes produced glowing or flaming effects in different materials, such as a flame over salt water, glowing silicon fragments, and a 33 cm ball of light on a steel surface, but Uman's group said these were not actual ball lightning, just interesting effects of different materials reacting to lightning.

Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.

questions.question: What did the 2012 spectroscopic recording of ball lightning on the Qinghai Plateau, China, reveal about its composition, and which theory did this support?
questions.referenceAnswer: The ball's spectrum showed lines from iron, calcium, silicon, nitrogen, and oxygen, elements consistent with soil, supporting the theory that ball lightning forms when lightning strikes the ground.

evidence.quote: The ball lightning spectrum showed lines due to Fe, CA, Si, N, and O consistent with the Abrahamson and Dinniss (2002) soil strike theory.

questions.question: In his conclusion, what does the author propose as a way to move ball lightning research beyond its current fragmented, individualized state?
questions.premise: Cases like the Qinghai spectroscopic recording provided rare physical evidence about ball lightning's nature.
questions.referenceAnswer: He calls for better-coordinated, systematic multidisciplinary documentation of cases, using physical-evidence benchmark cases together with digital material from mobile phones and webcams, to build a database against which theories and lab simulations can be critically tested.

evidence.quote: systematic multidisciplinary case documentation and discussion can lead to a database against which ball lightning theories and simulations can be critically assessed.

ideas.name: Expert witnesses are more trustworthy observers
ideas.statement: People with scientific training or a technical profession notice and later recall the details of a brief, strange event more accurately than an untrained bystander would.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: The entire project of singling out scientists, engineers, weather observers and doctors only makes sense if their accounts carry more evidential weight than ordinary eyewitness reports; the article never argues for this, it simply builds the whole collection on it.
ideas.analogy: It works like a courtroom giving extra weight to an expert witness's testimony because their training makes them a more reliable recorder of what happened.

occurrences.quote: As chances to monitor this transient phenomenon are low, it seems promising to evaluate observation reports by scientists and trained professionals.
occurrences.reasoning: States the paper's rationale for its whole sampling strategy without defending why expertise should improve testimony.

occurrences.quote: Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals.
occurrences.reasoning: Treats prior researchers' choice to privilege expert reports as self-evidently sound rather than something requiring justification.

occurrences.quote: It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.
occurrences.reasoning: Explicitly leans on the premise to justify including childhood memories of people who later became scientists, as if later training retroactively improves the original observation's credibility.

occurrences.quote: Weather observers of meteorological stations are trained and predestined to see and report transient weather phenomena.
occurrences.reasoning: Assumes without argument that a person's job training makes their chance sighting of an unpredictable event more credible evidence.

ideas.name: Aggregated reports describe one real external phenomenon
ideas.statement: Treating dozens of independent sightings as data points whose sizes, durations and timings can be averaged, ranged and compared only works if the reports are measurements of a single real physical thing and not unrelated illusions, mistakes, or distinct phenomena being mislabeled the same name.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: The statistical synthesis of means, medians, and ranges across the 41 cases presupposes that these numbers are describing a shared underlying object, not simply computing noise from many unrelated occurrences.

occurrences.quote: Reported observation durations (25 cases) range from 1.5 to 180 s with the maximum under 3 s but 5–6 cases in the higher categories. Mean is 19.5 s, standard deviation is 38.6, median is 4.0, and mode of 2.5 s.
occurrences.reasoning: Computing a mean and standard deviation across cases only makes sense if the underlying events are instances of the same kind of thing being measured.

occurrences.quote: Observation months follow the seasonal thunderstorm maximum – 7 July, 5 June/August each.
occurrences.reasoning: Treating the distribution of report months as a meaningful pattern assumes the reports track a real seasonal phenomenon rather than being an arbitrary collection of anecdotes.

occurrences.quote: even this relatively small sample of educated and trained observers shows a variety of situations, object sizes, and case durations, and some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model.
occurrences.reasoning: Calling some cases 'outliers' relative to 'one general ball lightning model' only makes sense if the whole set is assumed to be sampling from a single phenomenon with a central tendency.

ideas.name: A phenomenon can be real without having an accepted explanation
ideas.statement: The sheer volume and consistency of independent reports can justify treating something as a genuine natural phenomenon worth investigating, even while no theory for how it works has been agreed on and no laboratory has reliably reproduced it.

occurrences.quote: the consensus that “the reality of ball lightning is not in doubt.”
occurrences.reasoning: States plainly that a panel of researchers accepted the phenomenon as real despite the absence of a settled explanation.

occurrences.quote: With thousands of eyewitness reports, but few instrumental records and no consensus about a theory, ball lightning remains an unsolved problem in atmospheric physics.
occurrences.reasoning: Frames the situation as an 'unsolved problem' rather than a non-existent one, separating the question of reality from the question of explanation.

occurrences.quote: Regardless of all problems with an explanatory theory, detailed case reports should be documented.
occurrences.reasoning: Explicitly argues that documentation work should proceed independently of whether a satisfying theory exists.

ideas.name: Popular dramatic imagery gets mistaken for the real phenomenon
ideas.statement: Sensational, story-like depictions of dramatic deaths or destruction attributed to ball lightning have shaped public expectation of what it looks like, even where the underlying event was actually ordinary lightning.

occurrences.quote: However, a popular engraving pictured a lightning ball that hit Richmann. As in the 1818 Frankenstein novel, the grim fate of an avantgarde scientist sounded plausible. Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
occurrences.reasoning: States directly that a famous case long treated as ball lightning was actually conventional lightning, and that its dramatic retelling shaped the public image of the phenomenon.

occurrences.quote: Ball lightning cases also have a psychological side, when it comes to eyewitness quality, (non-)reporting, and public and media event labelling. Here, everyday life theories or mindsets are more influential than science.
occurrences.reasoning: Develops the point that media and folk narratives, not scientific criteria, often determine which events get labeled ball lightning.

ideas.name: Ball lightning may be several different phenomena, not one
ideas.statement: What gets called 'ball lightning' might actually be multiple distinct physical mechanisms that happen to look similar to observers, rather than a single effect awaiting one explanation.

occurrences.quote: There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated
occurrences.reasoning: States directly that the named phenomenon could be a grouping of several distinct effects.

occurrences.quote: This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning. Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a "ball lightning norm" and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition.
occurrences.reasoning: Develops the idea further by warning against forcing all cases into a single model and arguing instead for tolerating multiple types.

quotes.text: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probable ball lightning events.
quotes.reason: Concrete illustration of just how rare direct documentation is.

quotes.text: The unexpectedly high number of positive strokes and the equal frequency of close and distant events were discussed at the 34th International Conference on Lightning Protection.
quotes.reason: Key empirical result from the author's own lightning-location correlation study.

quotes.text: Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data
quotes.reason: A useful debunking note showing the author's care in distinguishing sourced reports from folklore.

quotes.text: His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom).
quotes.reason: Flags a genuinely puzzling physical anomaly in one of the strongest cases.

quotes.text: This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist. Gerlach is renowned for his 1922 experiment about spin quantization in a magnetic field.
quotes.reason: Highlights why Gerlach's account is especially credible and notable among the collected cases.

quotes.text: The tendency of weather services to do without observers and automate synoptic stations (including German mountaintop observatories) may be justified from an economic standpoint, but it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning.
quotes.reason: Raises a real cost of modernization: losing the trained human witnesses this whole review depends on.

quotes.text: Whether this will be compensated by citizen science and the spread of mobile phone and web cameras remains uncertain.
quotes.reason: Open question the author leaves hanging about the future of evidence-gathering.

quotes.text: Thus, even this relatively small sample of educated and trained observers shows a variety of situations, object sizes, and case durations, and some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model.
quotes.reason: Summarizes the statistical synthesis's main finding: diversity that resists a single explanation.

quotes.text: Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a “ball lightning norm” and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition.
quotes.reason: A methodological principle guarding against cherry-picking which cases count.

quotes.text: Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
quotes.reason: Explains how a famous but misattributed death case shaped public myth about ball lightning.

quotes.text: Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.
quotes.reason: An important caveat distinguishing a rigorous lab experiment from an actual ball lightning claim.

quotes.text: The main difference between modern science and Frankenstein’s laboratory is guiding research paradigms that – in the case of natural phenomena – condition a proper order of systematic data acquisition, formation, and testing of hypotheses and theories, and – if possible – laboratory simulation.
quotes.reason: The conceptual frame for why ball lightning research has struggled compared to normal science.

quotes.text: In the case of ball lightning, the research logic is distorted by a random phenomenon that is hard to observe, irreproducible, and mostly reported by change.
quotes.reason: Pinpoints exactly why the field has resisted standard scientific method.

quotes.text: Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests.
quotes.reason: Diagnoses the structural weakness of the field as fragmented and uncoordinated effort.

quotes.text: With physical evidence cases like the Dorstone tub, the Poughquag glass, or the Qinghai spectrum as benchmarks and digital material from abundantly present mobile phones and webcams, systematic multidisciplinary case documentation and discussion can lead to a database against which ball lightning theories and simulations can be critically assessed.
quotes.reason: The article's concluding prescription for how the field could finally make progress.

entries.name: Ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A rare, still-unexplained glowing sphere seen during thunderstorms, lasting a few seconds and vanishing with or without a trace. The article treats it as a real but poorly documented atmospheric phenomenon, not a myth, and focuses on reports from people trained to observe carefully.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: A 19th-century French astronomer and physicist whose 1837 writings on thunder first gave the phenomenon the name 'ball lightning' in French and German.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.senseHere: A US network of cameras that continuously photographed the night sky for over a decade to catch meteorites, which incidentally captured two probable ball lightning events among thousands of photos.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: Austria's network of ground sensors that detects and locates lightning strikes, letting researchers match reported ball lightning sightings to real, timed and located lightning strokes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: Germany's equivalent lightning-detection network, used the same way as ALDIS to confirm and time-stamp lightning strokes associated with reported ball lightning sightings.

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: A Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate who proposed a theoretical explanation for ball lightning, though the article notes he never reported having personally seen it.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: An Austrian geologist and mineralogist and member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna who recorded one of the earliest detailed scientific sightings of ball lightning, in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: A German astrophysicist at the Göttingen university observatory who, as a child in 1951, witnessed and later carefully documented a ball lightning event that broke apart into smaller glowing spheres.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: An American paleontology professor at Yale and president of the US National Academy of Sciences who witnessed and reported a ball lightning strike on a yacht in 1878.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: A German physics professor known for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment on magnetic spin, who later calculated a ball lightning object's speed from a 1927 sighting at Tübingen.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer, later a professor of physical electronics, whose 1963 account of a glowing sphere passing down an airplane aisle became a widely cited ball lightning report.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: An 18th-century Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who died in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity. Popular engravings wrongly depicted his death as caused by ball lightning, when records show it was an ordinary lightning strike through an ungrounded conductor.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A pioneering French neurologist at Paris's Salpêtrière Hospital who taught Sigmund Freud. He examined a patient's ball lightning encounter to distinguish its short-term nerve effects from lasting psychological trauma.

entries.name: Keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or numbness in a limb that follows a lightning or ball lightning encounter, distinct from any lasting nerve or psychological damage.

entries.name: Soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: An explanation proposing that ball lightning forms when a lightning strike vaporizes soil, releasing metal-rich vapor that burns and glows in a floating ball. The article notes a 2012 spectroscopic recording in China matched the chemical signature this theory predicts.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.background: A European research collaboration project on the physics of lightning, involving around 30 researchers, whose 2005 proposal stated a consensus that ball lightning's reality was not in doubt.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.senseHere: A frequently cited but thinly documented 1936 British account of a glowing ball crashing into a tub of water, used by researchers to estimate how much energy a ball lightning object might carry.

entries.name: Camp Blanding triggered-lightning experiment
entries.senseHere: A field test in which researchers deliberately triggered lightning strikes onto various ground materials to study the resulting glowing effects, concluding these were not true ball lightning but related materials phenomena.

entries.name: Qinghai Plateau spectroscopic recording
entries.senseHere: A 2012 Chinese field observation in which two cameras captured a ball lightning event's light spectrum right after a lightning strike hit the ground, giving rare chemical evidence about what the glowing ball was made of.

entries.text: Ball lightning remains unproven and unexplained; the claim here is that credible witnesses, not instruments, may be the way forward.
The name is over a century old, but after thousands of reports no theory or consensus has emerged.
Direct recordings are almost nonexistent, so the plan is to lean on trained witnesses and the author's own decades of fieldwork.
Dozens of firsthand accounts from physicists and professionals now give the phenomenon unusual credibility, even without physical proof.
Beyond scientists, further trained witnesses add weight but no more hard evidence to the same unsettled picture.
Pooling all 41 cases shows a real seasonal pattern but no single consistent shape, size, or behavior.
A handful of landmark cases offer rare physical traces and data, cutting through myth but still short of an explanation.
With evidence gathered but no theory confirmed, the call now is for coordinated collection to replace scattered individual efforts.
The sightings are documented and shared, but whether they can ever settle what ball lightning actually is remains open.
